modules.title: Power Automate automation fundamentals
modules.summary: Learn how Power Automate uses cloud flows, desktop flows, connectors, approvals, process mining, and AI-assisted creation.

lessons.title: Power Automate capabilities: cloud, desktop, process, and AI
lessons.summary: Choose the right Power Automate capability for event-driven cloud workflows, desktop RPA, approvals, process insights, and AI-assisted creation.
learningObjectives: Compare cloud flows, desktop flows, process mining, approvals, and AI Builder
Identify scheduled, automated, and instant cloud flow triggers
Explain when desktop RPA is useful for legacy apps
Choose the right Power Automate capability for a workflow scenario
lessons.explanation:
Ever feel like your workday is made of tiny copy-paste chores? **Power Automate** turns repeated steps into automations. At Contoso Facilities, one request might arrive from Microsoft Forms, another from SharePoint, and a third from Dataverse. Instead of asking a coordinator to watch every inbox, a cloud flow can start from an event, run on demand, or run on a schedule.

**Cloud flows** run in the Power Automate service. An automated cloud flow starts when an event happens, an instant cloud flow starts when a user selects a button, and a scheduled cloud flow starts on a timer. Cloud flows use **connectors** for services such as Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Forms, and Dataverse.

**Desktop flows** add robotic process automation for rule-based tasks on a workstation, especially where a legacy app has no modern API. Use desktop flows when the work is repetitive and UI-based; use cloud flows when work is event-driven across connected services.

Power Automate also includes approvals for human decisions, **process mining** for discovering bottlenecks from event data, document automation scenarios, and Copilot experiences that help makers describe or modify flows in natural language. You will practise this foundation in the **Build an approval cloud flow in Power Automate** lab.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso Facilities wants cloud flows for Dataverse requests, desktop flows for a legacy label app, and process mining to identify repair bottlenecks.
lessons.technicalExample: Choose automated for Dataverse row created, instant for a manager button, scheduled for Friday summaries, desktop for legacy UI, and process mining for event-log analysis.

misconception.myth: Every Power Automate scenario should be solved with an automated cloud flow.
misconception.reality: Automated cloud flows are great for service events, but instant flows, scheduled flows, desktop flows, approvals, and process mining each solve different problems.

lessons.examTakeaway: If the clue is a clock, choose scheduled; if it is a user button, choose instant; if it is a service event, choose automated; if it is a legacy desktop screen, choose desktop flow/RPA; if it is bottleneck discovery, choose process mining.
lessons.recap: Choose the right Power Automate capability for event-driven cloud workflows, desktop RPA, approvals, process insights, and AI-assisted creation.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of Power Automate like a transport hub: some trains leave on a timetable, some taxis are called by a person, some alarms dispatch automatically, and a courier handles awkward old routes that have no modern connection.
lessons.anotherExample: Litware uses an automated flow when a SharePoint request is created, an instant flow for a supervisor reminder button, a scheduled flow for Friday summaries, a desktop flow for a legacy badge printer, and process mining to find approval delays.

lessons.title: Build a basic cloud flow with triggers, actions, and testing
lessons.summary: Learn the parts of a basic cloud flow: triggers, actions, dynamic content, conditions, approvals, testing, and run history.
learningObjectives: Identify triggers, actions, dynamic content, conditions, and approvals in a cloud flow
Describe how run history and testing help troubleshoot a flow
Explain how branches handle approval outcomes
Choose flow steps for a basic event-driven business process
lessons.explanation:
A good cloud flow feels like a tiny assembly line: something starts it, each station does a job, and the run history tells you what happened. In Contoso's approval-flow lab, a new equipment request row in Dataverse is the **trigger**.

The trigger is the starting event. A connector provides triggers and actions. **Actions** are the steps after the trigger: create an approval, post a Teams message, send an email, update a row, or call another service. Many actions use **dynamic content**, which is data from the trigger or earlier steps.

Conditions make flows useful for real business logic. If the approval outcome is Approve, update Status to Approved; otherwise, update Status to Rejected. Copilot can help create and modify cloud flows from natural language, but you still need to review the design.

Testing is not optional. Use the flow checker where available, run a test with realistic data, and inspect **run history** to see status, start time, duration, and failed steps. You will practise these ideas in the **Build an approval cloud flow in Power Automate** lab.

terminology.definition: The event or schedule that starts a cloud flow.
A step that performs work after the trigger.
Values from previous steps used later.
Records used to review and troubleshoot runs.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso Facilities wants every equipment request approved before purchasing acts.
lessons.technicalExample: Trigger: Dataverse row added; Action: Start and wait for approval; Condition: Outcome equals Approve; Update status; Send email; Test; Review run history.

misconception.myth: A saved cloud flow is ready for production because the designer accepted it.
misconception.reality: A saved design can still fail because of missing connections, wrong dynamic content, bad branch logic, or unexpected data; testing and run history prove behavior.

lessons.examTakeaway: For build questions, separate the parts: the trigger starts, actions do work, dynamic content carries values, conditions branch, approvals wait for people, and run history explains each run.
lessons.recap: Learn the parts of a basic cloud flow: triggers, actions, dynamic content, conditions, approvals, testing, and run history.
lessons.simplerExplanation: A cloud flow is like a parcel route: the pickup request starts it, labels carry information from stop to stop, a sorting gate chooses the lane, and the tracking page shows where the parcel got stuck.
lessons.anotherExample: Proseware builds a purchase request flow that starts from a Microsoft Forms response, uses the requester name in a Teams approval, branches on Approve or Reject, and checks run history after a test submission.
